Variant Records in ClinVar

Two additional records—"NM_000041.4(APOE):c.[388=;526=]" [1] and "NM_000041.3(APOE):c.[349G>A;508G>C]" [2]. 

Gene records found

gene symbol: APOE [3]. gene name: APOE [5]. The protein encoded by this gene is a major apoprotein of the chylomicron [10]. It binds to a specific liver and peripheral cell receptor, and is essential for the normal catabolism of triglyceride-rich lipoprotein constituents [10]. This gene maps to chromosome 19 in a cluster with the related apolipoprotein C1 and C2 genes [10]. Mutations in this gene result in familial dysbetalipoproteinemia, or type III hyperlipoproteinemia (HLP III), in which increased plasma cholesterol and triglycerides are the conseque [10]. 

Pubmed records found

pubmed title: APOE in the normal brain [4]. pubmed title: Overexpressing low-density lipoprotein receptor reduces tau-associated neurodegeneration in relation to apoE-linked mechanisms [9]. pubmed title: Apolipoprotein E and Alzheimer's disease [14]. pubmed title: Apolipoprotein E secreted by astrocytes forms antiparallel dimers in discoidal lipoproteins [19]. pubmed title: Silencing Apoe with divalent-siRNAs improves amyloid burden and activates immune response pathways in Alzheimer's disease [24]. The APOE4 protein affects the primary neuropathological markers of Alzheimer's disease (AD): amyloid plaques, neurofibrillary tangles, and gliosis [29]. These interactions have been investigated to understand the strong effect of APOE genotype on risk of AD [29]. However, APOE genotype has strong effects on processes in normal brains, in the absence of the hallmarks of AD [29]. We propose that CNS APOE is involved in processes in the normal brains that in later years apply specifically to processes of AD patho [29]. APOE is the strongest genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease [31]. ApoE exacerbates tau-associated neurodegeneration by driving microglial activation [31]. However, how apoE regulates microglial activation and whether targeting apoE is therapeutically beneficial in tauopathy is unclear [31]. Here, we show that overexpressing an apoE metabolic receptor, LDLR (low-density lipoprotein receptor), in P301S tauopathy mice markedly reduces brain apoE and ameliorates tau pathology and neurodegeneration [31]. Genetic variation in apolipoprotein E (APOE) influences Alzheimer's disease (AD) risk [33]. APOE ε4 alleles are the strongest genetic risk factor for late onset sporadic AD [33]. The AD risk is dose dependent, as those carrying one APOE ε4 allele have a 2-3-fold increased risk, while those carrying two ε4 alleles have a 10-15-fold increased risk [33]. Individuals carrying APOE ε2 alleles have lower AD risk and those carrying APOE ε3 alleles have neutral risk [33]. APOE is a lipoprotein which functions in lipid tran [33]. The Apolipoprotein E gene (APOE) is of great interest due to its role as a risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease [35]. ApoE is secreted by astrocytes in the central nervous system in high-density lipoprotein (HDL)-like lipoproteins [35]. Structural models of lipidated ApoE of high resolution could aid in a mechanistic understanding of how ApoE functions in health and disease [35]. Using monoclonal Fab and F(ab')2 fragments, we characterize the structure of lipidated ApoE on astrocyte-secreted lipoprot [35]. The most significant genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease (AD) is APOE4, with evidence for gain- and loss-of-function mechanisms [37]. A clinical need remains for therapeutically relevant tools that potently modulate APOE expression [37]. We optimized small interfering RNAs (di-siRNA, GalNAc) to potently silence brain or liver Apoe and evaluated the impact of each pool of Apoe on pathology [37]. In adult 5xFAD mice, siRNAs targeting CNS Apoe efficiently silenced Apoe expression and reduced am [37].
